title: Scotland Win Their First World Cup Match in 36 Years as McGinn Deflection Sinks Haiti
excerpt: John McGinn's 28th-minute strike — via a fortunate deflection — gives Steve Clarke's men a priceless 1-0 victory at Gillette Stadium
body:
## The Tartan Army Returns — And Wins

It had been 36 years. The last time Scotland won a World Cup match, Margaret Thatcher was still in Downing Street, the Berlin Wall had just fallen, and Mo Johnston's penalty against Sweden in Italia '90 was the moment of triumph. On a warm Saturday evening in Foxborough, Massachusetts, John McGinn's deflected strike finally gave Scotland something they had waited more than three decades to celebrate.

## McGinn Breaks the Deadlock

The first quarter-hour was tense and open. Scott McTominay, ever the box-to-box presence in Scotland's midfield, signalled his intent early with a header that sailed over in the 7th minute. Both sides started brightly — Louicius Deedson dragged a shot wide for Haiti and nearly picked out Wilson Isidor with a dangerous cross.

Then, in the 17th minute, McTominay came agonisingly close. He rattled the post with a first-time right-footed strike from Ben Gannon-Doak's cross, with goalkeeper Johny Placide rooted to the spot. The woodwork was all that stood between Scotland and the lead.

They would not have to wait long. In the 28th minute, Che Adams drove towards the Haiti goal and forced a save from Placide. The ball fell to McGinn, whose shot took a deflection off a Haitian defender and looped over the scrambling goalkeeper. It was scrappy, it was fortunate — and it was Scotland's first World Cup goal since Craig Burley's equaliser against Norway in 1998.

McGinn had earned the right to be the man delivering it. Less than a month earlier, he had lifted the Europa League trophy as captain of Aston Villa. Now he was scoring at a World Cup. The Tartan Army — Scotland's famously loyal travelling supporters — were in full throat, having already delivered a lung-busting rendition of "The Bonnie Banks of Loch Lomond" before kickoff.

## Haiti's Frustration Mounts

For Haiti, playing in their first World Cup since 1974, the scoreline did not reflect their performance. They actually outshot Scotland 8-7 in the first half, with possession roughly even. Two Premier League-based players — Jean-Ricner Bellegarde of Wolverhampton Wanderers and Sunderland's Wilson Isidor — brought quality and ambition to every Haitian attack.

But the offside flag was a persistent enemy. Multiple scoring chances were nullified by tight calls, and when Haiti did create clean openings, they lacked the finishing touch. Wilson Isidor got his head on a free-kick cross in the first half but could not find the target.

The second half was more subdued. Scotland, protecting their lead, sat deeper and let Haiti have the ball in non-threatening areas. Steve Clarke's men were disciplined but not entirely comfortable — they collected three yellow cards in the second half as Haiti pushed forward.

Haiti's best chances to equalise came in the final 15 minutes. In the 74th minute, Ruben Providence's cross from the left narrowly missed Isidor for a back-post deflection. Then Frantzdy Pierrot, who had come on as a substitute, found space between two Scottish defenders and leapt highest for Carlens Arcus's cross — but his header spun agonisingly wide of the left post.

## The Historical Weight

The numbers tell the story of Scottish World Cup futility: this was their ninth tournament appearance, and until Saturday, they had won just four of their 23 World Cup matches — all of them in 1990 or earlier. A generation of Scottish supporters had grown up knowing their team only in the context of gallant defeats and group-stage eliminations.

McGinn's goal was the first for Scotland at a World Cup since Craig Burley's strike against Norway in France '98. The current ESPN pundit probably never imagined he would hold that particular record for 28 years.

## From Foxborough to Foxborough

For Greater Boston's desi community — the tech workers of Cambridge, the students along Route 128, the families of the western suburbs — this was the World Cup on their doorstep. Gillette Stadium, which had not hosted a World Cup match since the tournament's 1994 debut at the old Foxboro Stadium next door, provided a fitting backdrop for Scotland's milestone moment.

## Group C Implications

Scotland's three points put them atop Group C after Brazil and Morocco played out a 1-1 draw earlier in the day. It is the best possible start for Clarke's men, who face a far sterner test when they meet Morocco back at Gillette Stadium on Friday, June 19. Haiti, meanwhile, head to Philadelphia to take on Brazil — a daunting proposition, but one they will approach knowing they were far from disgraced here.

At a 48-team World Cup where three points and a decent goal difference should be enough to reach the last 32, Scotland have given themselves an excellent platform. For a nation that has never progressed beyond the group stage, that is not nothing.
